audit.evidence: The 5.7L HEMI broken exhaust manifold bolt issue is extensively documented across owner forums, a Chrysler TSB (11-002-11 for the 2009 DS Ram 1500), and dealer/warranty blogs spanning 2009-2022+ model years, with the classic cold-start ticking that quiets when warm caused by thermal cycling between the aluminum head and iron manifold. However, P0420/P0430 are catalytic converter efficiency codes not typically associated with this specific failure mode, which most often presents as a noise complaint without DTCs.

issues_found: Severity 'high' is borderline - this is primarily a costly mechanical failure rather than safety-critical; could arguably be 'medium' per the provided definitions where high=safety-critical and medium=costly but not dangerous
audit.evidence: The 5.7L HEMI MDS lifter/cam failure is extensively documented across forums (RamForum, Allpar, CarComplaints) and repair sites for multiple model years of the 5.7L HEMI, including the 1500 Classic platform which uses the same Eagle 5.7L engine as earlier 4th-gen trucks. Repair costs commonly cited at $3,350-$5,300 (cam + all 16 lifters), and misfire DTCs P0301-P0308 plus P0300 are the correct codes per multiple sources including cararac.com which explicitly lists P0300-P0308 for this failure.

results.title: MDS Lifter Failure and Hemi Tick (5.7L)

issues_found: Severity 'high' is debatable - this is more of a costly mechanical failure than a safety-critical issue, though severe lifter failure with cam damage can disable the vehicle
DTC list is comprehensive but P0300 (random misfire) is the most commonly cited; cylinder-specific codes depend on which lifter fails
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (forums, repair guides, and a P0300 diagnostic database covering 2019-2026 Ram 1500) confirm MDS lifter failure and 'Hemi tick' as a widely documented issue on the 5.7L Hemi, with P0300 and cylinder-specific misfire codes being the typical DTCs and severe cases requiring camshaft replacement. Repair cost estimates from sources range from $1,200-$2,500 for lifters/solenoids up to ~$5,000 for full cam-and-lifter jobs, consistent with the $2,000-$4,500 estimate.

issues_found: Year range is significantly off: documented delamination predominantly affects 2017-2019 (especially 2018) model years with the bad LG LA084X01(SL)(01) screen; Stellantis switched to improved (02) screen for 2020+ and reports drop off sharply
No evidence of widespread delamination on 5th gen (2025) RAM 2500s — claim of '4th and 5th gen' affected appears fabricated
12-inch screen delamination is not documented as a common issue; reports overwhelmingly involve the 8.4-inch Uconnect 4 unit

Severity 'low' is arguably miscategorized — owners and ClassAction.org report phantom touches causing radio/HVAC/backup camera to activate unprompted while driving, which is a potential safety distraction
Repair cost upper bound slightly low — dealer quotes commonly cited at $1,500-$2,500 for full unit replacement
No NHTSA recall or official Stellantis TSB issued; described primarily through owner forums and a closed class-action investigation
audit.evidence: Uconnect 8.4 touchscreen delamination is a widely documented defect on 2017-2019 FCA/Stellantis vehicles including RAM 2500 (especially 2018), with bubbling, rainbow distortion, and phantom touches caused by failing digitizer adhesive. However, the issue is tied to a specific LG screen part used in 2018-2019, was largely resolved with a revised part in 2020+, and there is no credible evidence of the issue affecting 2022-2025 RAM 2500s or the 12-inch Uconnect 5 screens.

issues_found: Repair costs can exceed $1500 if bolts break during removal (dealer quotes up to $3000); range is slightly conservative on the high end
Description specifies cylinders #3 and #4 as crack location, but forum/vendor reports more commonly cite rear cylinders (#5, #6) as failure points
audit.evidence: Multiple aftermarket vendors (BD Diesel, DPS, XDP) and Cummins owner forums confirm the one-piece cast iron exhaust manifold on 6.7L Cummins RAM 2500/3500 trucks is notorious for cracking due to heat cycling, producing cold-start ticking that fades when warm, with both 4th gen (2007.5-2018) and 5th gen (2019-2024) designs affected. Repair cost estimates from JustAnswer cite ~$650 in parts plus ~$1000 labor (~$1650 total), with dealer quotes reaching $3000 when bolts break.

issues_found: Repair cost range ($200-$600) is somewhat low compared to RepairPal's $610-$722 estimate for professional replacement
Description claims factory U-joints are 'undersized' - the documented root cause on 2013+ aluminum driveshafts is galvanic corrosion from incorrect U-joint coating, not undersizing
Many factory U-joints on these trucks are sealed/non-greaseable (no zerk fittings), so the maintenance-overlooked grease fitting claim is misleading for newer years
Year range is very broad; issue characteristics differ between 2nd-gen carryover designs and 4th-gen (2013+) aluminum driveshaft trucks
audit.evidence: Premature U-joint failure is well documented on RAM 2500s across forums (RamForum, CumminsForum, DodgeForum) and CarComplaints, and a MOOG technical bulletin specifically addresses 2013-2018 RAM 2500/3500 aluminum driveshaft U-joint failures from galvanic corrosion. RepairPal lists average replacement cost at $610-$722, slightly above the entry's stated range.

issues_found: Transfer case model numbers 'BW4470' and 'BW4494' appear fabricated - actual BorgWarner units in RAM 2500 are designated BW 44-44, BW 44-45, BW 44-46, and BW 48-series
Year range incorrect: 2010-2011 RAM 2500s used New Venture Gear transfer cases (NV241/NV271/NV273), not BorgWarner. BorgWarner units began appearing in RAM HD trucks around 2012-2013
Repair cost likely understated - dealer reseal/output shaft seal repairs commonly run higher, especially when case halves must be separated
Issue is more prominently reported on recent (2023-2024) model year trucks than across the entire claimed range
audit.evidence: Forum reports (Cummins Forum, RamForum) confirm real, ongoing transfer case output shaft seal and case-half leak issues on RAM 2500 trucks, with multiple owners reporting repeat warranty repairs and back-ordered seals described as a 'known issue.' However, the specific part numbers BW4470/BW4494 do not match BorgWarner's actual designations (BW 44-44/44-45/44-46/48-xx), and the 2010-2011 years used New Venture Gear NV-series transfer cases instead.

issues_found: Description states center studs (#3 and #4) fail most frequently, but documented evidence indicates the rear cylinders (closer to #5/#6) run hottest and are typically where failures originate first
Repair cost upper bound ($1200) may be slightly low — documented quotes range up to $1650-$3200 when broken studs must be extracted from the head or manifold is also replaced

Year range starts at 2010 but the 6.7L Cummins has been in Ram trucks since 2007.5; not technically wrong for the listed vehicle years but the issue is well-documented across the entire 2007.5-2024 platform
audit.evidence: Multiple aftermarket suppliers (BD Diesel, Diesel Power Source, Mishimoto, Pure Diesel Power) and owner forums confirm broken exhaust manifold studs/bolts and cracked manifolds are a very common, well-documented issue on the 6.7L Cummins due to thermal cycling, with rear cylinders running hottest. No DTCs are typically set (consistent with the entry), and repair costs in forums range from ~$400 to $3200 depending on broken stud extraction difficulty.

issues_found: Description conflates in-bed 7-pin (gooseneck prep) with 4-pin connector; the factory in-bed prep connector is 7-pin only — 4-pin is at the rear bumper, not under the bed
Auxiliary camera dropouts are not typically routed through the in-bed gooseneck prep harness, so that symptom is likely inaccurate

No manufacturer TSB or recall specifically documents in-bed gooseneck prep harness corrosion as a systemic defect; evidence is anecdotal forum reports and general 7-pin corrosion (often at the rear bumper splice, not the in-bed connector specifically)
Year range is broad but defensible; prep package availability and connector style changed around 2010, so 2013-2025 is reasonable
audit.evidence: Forum threads (Cummins Forum, RamForumZ) and parts vendor pages confirm 7-pin trailer connector corrosion is a common, well-known nuisance on RAM 2500/3500 trucks, frequently at the bumper splice junction where the harness tees to the bed connector, with dielectric grease and connector cleaning as typical fixes. However, no manufacturer TSB or NHTSA documentation isolates the in-bed gooseneck prep connector specifically as a defect, and the description's mention of an under-bed 4-pin connector and camera dropouts does not match the actual factory wiring architecture.

results.title: Front Hub Bearing Failure Under Heavy Load

issues_found: DTC codes C0050/C0051 are not the standard codes associated with RAM 3500 wheel bearing failures; documented codes are typically wheel speed sensor codes like C003A and C0037, or generic 'implausible wheel speed' ABS codes
Severity 'medium' may be undercalibrated — multiple owner reports describe wheel detachment, hub disintegration at highway speed, and loss of steering control, which is safety-critical
Mileage range 60,000-100,000 is plausible but real-world failures span 39K to 180K miles, so the range is narrower than reality
Repair cost $300-$700 is reasonable for the front hub assembly on a 3500 but may be slightly low for dealer-performed work on a 4x4 HD truck
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forum threads (Cummins Forum, RamForumZ, RamForum) confirm widespread front hub bearing failures on 4th-gen RAM 3500 (2010+) trucks, with documented failures at 39K, 58K, 70K, 87K, 89K, and 114K miles. A 2021 RAM 3500 TSB specifically addresses front Hub/Bearing growling/humming noise, leaking grease, and excessive play, and NHTSA has prior wheel bearing recalls/complaints on Ram platforms — but the cited DTCs C0050/C0051 do not match the wheel-speed-sensor codes (C003A, C0037) documented in FCA TSBs for this condition.

issues_found: DTC codes P0540 and P0543 are generic intake air heater circuit codes but the most commonly documented codes for this specific RAM 6.7L issue are P2609 and P0542, not P0540/P0543

Severity may be under-calibrated: NHTSA recall Y08/Y76 exists for 2021-2022 RAM trucks where stuck-on relays cause fire risk (safety-critical), and the related 'killer bolt' failure mode can cause catastrophic engine damage
Year range starts at 2010 but the 6.7L Cummins was introduced in 2007.5; issue is documented for 2007-2024 model years
Repair cost range ($80-$250) may be low if TSB-recommended repair (replacing both grid heater and relay as a set) is followed, which can run $250-$350 OEM
audit.evidence: Banks Power, Cummins Forum, RamForum, and an NHTSA recall (Y08/Y76 for 2021-2022 trucks) confirm grid heater relay failure is a well-documented issue on 6.7L Cummins RAM trucks from 2007-2024, with Mopar TSB #9003585 addressing it for 2012-2016 models. However, the most commonly cited DTCs are P2609 and P0542 rather than the P0540/P0543 listed in the entry.

results.title: Rear Cargo Door Hinge Pin Wear and Door Sag

issues_found: Most documented hinge/door-sag complaints are for the full-size ProMaster (front driver door, A-pillar cracking) rather than the ProMaster City's rear cargo doors specifically
The specific claim that the 'upper driver-side rear hinge fails first' is not corroborated by TSBs or forum posts for the ProMaster City
No specific TSB found for ProMaster City rear hinge pin wear; the known TSB (MC-10214627) covers a driver-door check strap, not rear hinges
Repair cost range may be low — a single OEM rear upper hinge alone retails around $345+, so replacing multiple hinges with labor could exceed $600
audit.evidence: Mopar sells a dedicated door hinge pin (PN 68266393AA) for 2015-2022 ProMaster City, and forum users report rear hinge pins wearing/becoming sloppy and affecting door alignment, confirming the general phenomenon. However, most prominent hinge-failure discussions and the related NHTSA TSB pertain to the full-size ProMaster's front driver door, not the ProMaster City's rear cargo doors, and the specific 'upper driver-side fails first' detail is not documented.

results.title: 9-Speed Automatic Transmission Harsh Shifting and Hesitation

issues_found: Upper repair cost range ($2,500) is low - full transmission replacement on ProMaster City typically runs $3,500-$11,000 per dealer/owner reports
Description references 'FCA/Stellantis TCM software updates' generally without citing a specific TSB number, which weakens specificity
Owner forums note slow downshifts and reluctance to use 8th/9th gears more than 'harsh 1-2/2-3 shifts' specifically - symptom description is partially generic ZF 9HP boilerplate
audit.evidence: The ProMaster City does use the 948TE 9-speed (ZF 9HP derivative) across all 2015-2022 model years, and owner forums (promasterforum.com) plus industry sources (Transmission Digest, Northampton Transmission) document harsh shifting, slow downshifts, torque converter failures, and TCM-related drivability issues. However, owner-reported replacement costs frequently exceed $3,500-$11,000, making the stated $2,500 upper bound too low.
